newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak bank sees no strategy change yet.
newsitem.headline: Slovak bank sees no strategy change yet.

text.p: IRB a.s., Slovakia's third largest bank, does not anticipate making any major policy changes despite a recent shuffle of its board members, a senior bank officials told Reuters on Thursday.

"We further intend to be a development bank from our economy's point of view, but also an investment bank," said Frantisek Orolin, IRB Vice-president for treasury and the only board member to remain through the changes.
"Not earnings results, but provision creation for inherited risky assets remains the priority...which will not effect clients though. Our services will be at least at the current standard," he added.
Orolin said some two to four weeks were needed for the new board members' ideas to be "significantly tailor-made to IRB".
Last Thursday, IRB said it had replaced its president and three other board members upon request by its majority owners, but has not elaborated further on the move.
IRB's loan portfolio has a high share of classified loans, mainly those extended in the past for the completion of construction of the government's controversial Mochovce nuclear power plant.

Orolin said the IRB has been adhering closely to its three-year loan portfolio restructuring programme, creating provisions above central bank requirements. It hopes to have a clean portfolio by the end of 1998, he said.
"But while we will be (further) settling some old matters to over required levels, our capital adequacy as it is and our assets will fluctuate," he said.
IRB's capital adequacy ratio currently ranges within roughly 7.8-8.25 percent, Orolin said. The central bank requires a capital adequacy ratio of at least 8.0 percent.
Orolin said steel maker VSZ, IRB's private shareholder with a 14.6 percent stake, had not used the bank lending activities inappropriately.
"VSZ is not our largest client...though it is a top client within the Slovak economy. Commercial relations with it are based on real revenues, on real profits," Orolin said.

"VSZ has neither used or misused its position of one of the bank's owners -- we have no (new) deals, no new credits with them at the present -- though I consider commercial relations with them only attractive," he added.
VSZ recently took control of one-third of the seats on IRB's supervisory board and has been embroiled in a dispute with the central bank over its ambitions to control IRB.
The central bank has insisted on a reversal of the changes to both boards.
